### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Gao and colleagues deliver a statewide, seven-year descriptive portrait of midyear school mobility among California students in foster care, built on the CALPADS–CWS/CMS record match (133,127 students, roughly 304,000 student-years, 2017–18 through 2023–24), and the descriptive half of the paper holds up well: 31% of students in care change schools within a year against 6% of all students (p.5; Table 3), the gradient by grade band, race, disability and homelessness is reported faithfully (Table 3), about two-thirds of school moves coincide with a residential ZIP-code change (Table 3, Col. B), the rate fell from about 36% before the pandemic to about 30% in 2023–24 with the decline concentrated among students who move more than once (Figure 1), and later moves are increasingly likely to land in alternative settings (Table 6). Those facts are the reason to cite the paper, and they are new in one important respect — a consistent series that runs through the pandemic — though not in the respect the paper claims: WestEd's 2013 *Invisible Achievement Gap* report used the same state linkage to establish the one-third within-year mobility rate and the roughly 10% share attending three or more schools more than a decade ago, and the paper neither cites it nor benchmarks against it, so the "first large-scale longitudinal analysis" framing (pp.2, 11) should be discounted. The paper's other headline claims deserve more caution than the abstract signals. The "more than 20 miles" distance is a median over residential moves that changed ZIP code (Table 5), which drops the shortest moves by construction, and the text repeatedly calls it an average. The RQ4 regression (Table 8) is an adjusted description that the paper labels "Effects": its dominant regressor, a same-year residential change (+45 pp), is jointly determined with the outcome and the authors concede they cannot order the two events (p.5); the preferred sample retains only 203,095 of 304,466 student-years with no account of the loss (Table A3); and the community-level coefficients that carry the policy discussion are estimated with student-clustered standard errors on county- and district-level regressors and change sign across the paper's own specification ladder. The most consequential lapse is that the Discussion recommends "improving housing affordability" to reduce mobility (p.13) when the paper's own estimate runs the other way — a higher affordability index, meaning more affordable housing (p.11), is associated with more mobility (+.0013, Table 8, Col. A) — and that estimate reverses to −.0021 when Los Angeles is excluded (Table A3). Add a literature review that misattributes or garbles several citations, a set of exhibits whose units and denominators cannot be reconciled from what is printed (identical Ns across the residential-move and school-move tables; destination shares that exceed the mover rate; a three-year window defined for every year of a seven-year panel), and code available only to CDE-approved users, and the right posture is: rely on Tables 3–6 and Figure 1 as the current reference numbers for California, attach caveats to the distance and alternative-setting claims, and do not cite the community-factor findings or the policy recommendations built on them without reading Tables 8, 9 and A3–A6 directly.

#### Key Strengths

- Population-scale linked administrative data with a stated match rate (about 94%, p.3) covering every student touched by foster care in California for seven consecutive years, including the pandemic — the only consistent before/during/after series available for this population, and one that state agencies will act on given the CDE co-authorship.
- A clearly defined, well-motivated outcome. Within-year mobility is defined by primary enrollment records with named exclusions (dropouts, suspensions, stays of five days or fewer, summer moves, concurrent enrollment; p.4 and appendix p.16), the between-year alternative is quantified (31% rises to 35%; p.4), and comparison rates for other high-need groups are supplied (p.5).
- Descriptive exhibits that practitioners can use directly: mobility by race, grade band and need category (Table 3), by number and destination of moves (Table 4, A2), by school-type transition and move order (Table 6), and by year (Figure 1, Table A1). Two of these — the move-order gradient into alternative settings (traditional-to-traditional falls from 72% of first moves to 54% of third-plus moves) and the ZIP-to-ZIP residential distance measure — are genuinely new for California.
- A transparent specification ladder (Table A3) that adds covariate blocks one at a time, then county fixed effects, then drops Los Angeles, with a sample size for every column. The fragility findings in this review are visible only because the authors published that table.
- Honest scoping in the places that matter: the limits of the ZIP-code distance measure are stated immediately after the method (pp.4–5), the qualitative component is explicitly not presented as findings (p.4), and the paper says plainly that it cannot answer the school-of-origin question federal and state policy actually pose (p.13).

#### Key Concerns

- The regression is descriptive but is written as causal, and its main regressor is co-determined with the outcome. Table 8 is titled "Effects," residential change is "a major driver" (abstract) that "increases the probability" of a move (p.11), yet p.5 states the authors cannot tell whether the school change came before or after the home change. The +.4499 marginal effect largely restates the descriptive fact that two-thirds of school moves coincide with a residence change; conditioning on it also nets the other coefficients of the placement-instability channel (homelessness falls from .1783 to .0674 and Black from .0441 to .0281 when it enters; Table A3, though the sample also changes at that step).
- The community-level findings that carry the abstract and the policy discussion are fragile and over-precise. Standard errors are clustered at the student level (Table 8 note) while the housing affordability index, facility counts and STRTP share vary only at the county-year level and district poverty at the district-year level; with county fixed effects those coefficients are identified from within-county changes over at most seven years. Across Table A3 the affordability coefficient goes +.0021, +.0013, −.0021 (without LA); total facilities goes +.0095 to −.0387 when county FE enter; school % multilingual goes −.0319 to +.0305. The text nonetheless says "most of the estimates are consistent across specifications" (p.9), which is true only of the student-level block.
- The housing-affordability recommendation contradicts the paper's own estimate. HAI is the share of households able to afford a median-priced home (p.11); its coefficient is positive in the preferred model (+.0013, Table 8, Col. A), in all three periods of Table 9, and in the post-COVID interaction (Table A6). More affordable counties or years show more mobility, yet p.13 concludes that reducing mobility "should also focus on ... improving housing affordability." The child-poverty story fares better (post-COVID .2070 in Table 9; interaction .1745 in Table A6, both p<.01) but is explained with a national Supplemental Poverty Measure trend that the SAIPE official-measure regressor does not track, and a statewide time shock is absorbed by the year fixed effects in any case.
- The literature review is thin and in places inaccurate, and the novelty claims are overstated. Barrat and Berliner (2013, WestEd) — same linkage, one-third within-year mobility, just under 10% in three or more schools, disproportionate nontraditional enrollment — is absent from the reference list; the cited 2025 WestEd follow-up reports a decade of improving school stability but is used only for outcome gaps (p.1); Hanushek, Kain and Rivkin (2004) is cited for a midyear-timing claim their paper does not support for movers; Cutuli et al. (2013) is a homeless/highly-mobile study presented as foster-care evidence; the Gustavsson and MacEachron (2012) entry gives the wrong journal (it is *Children & Schools* 34(2), not *Children and Youth Services Review* 34(12)); and the "Kemp & Bodonyi (2000)" entry appears to merge two sources.
- Exhibits whose units and denominators cannot be reconciled as printed, plus roughly a third of the sample vanishing without comment. Table 1 pairs 133,127 unique foster students with 43,223,355 "All Students," which can only be student-years. Tables 5, 6 and A2 report the identical N row (49,913 / 20,316 / 9,041) whether the unit is a residential move or a school move, and those Ns imply 41% of first movers move again against Table 4's roughly 32%. Table 4's destination rows (9% + 16% + 12% = 37%) exceed the 31% who moved. Table 3, Col. C and Table A1 report a "3-year" rate for every year of a seven-year panel with no window definition. Table 2's "State" row (2,929 students in care) matches no statewide figure. And the preferred regression uses 203,095 of 304,466 student-years (Table A3) with no missingness analysis; Table 8's own three columns have three different Ns (203,095 / 207,042 / 207,046). Do-files go only to CDE-approved users, so none of this can be resolved by an outside replicator.

#### What to Rely On

- The pooled within-year mobility rate for students in foster care in California, 2017–18 to 2023–24: 31%, about five times the 6% rate for all students and roughly double the 16% rate for students experiencing homelessness (p.5; Table 3, Col. A). Read "in foster care" as "in care on any day of the school year" (p.3), so some counted moves precede entry or follow exit.
- The subgroup gradient: grades 9–12 (38%) above K–5 (27%); Black students (36%) above White (31%), Latino (30%) and Asian (23%); students experiencing homelessness (50%) far above all others; students with disabilities (34%) modestly above the mean (Table 3). Use Table 3 or the Base column of Table A3 for total gaps, not Table 8, whose student coefficients are conditional on a residential move.
- The trend: about 36% in both pre-pandemic years, a trough near 23% in 2020–21, and about 30% in 2023–24, with the decline concentrated among students moving more than once (14% in 2017–18 to 10% in 2023–24; Figure 1, p.8). Three-year mobility fell from 58% to 44% over the same window (Table A1).
- Roughly two-thirds of midyear school moves coincide with a same-year residential ZIP-code change (67%; Table 3, Col. B), higher for K–5 (70%) and students experiencing homelessness (75%). This corroborates the Colorado placement-record evidence in Clemens et al. (2017) in a second state; it does not establish sequence or cause.
- Later midyear moves are more likely to involve alternative settings: traditional-to-traditional falls from 72% of first moves to 54% of third-plus moves, and alternative-to-alternative rises from 7% to 18% (Table 6, Panel A). Cross-district and cross-county destinations outnumber within-district ones (Table 4; Table A2). Both patterns are partly mechanical (a detention-and-release sequence through a juvenile court school counts as two moves; county-run schools may carry their own district codes), so cite the pattern, not a mechanism.
- Residential moves that change ZIP code are typically long: median 22.5 miles for the first such move, 27.1 for the second, 29.8 for the third, rising to 35 miles for third moves in 2023–24 (Table 5; Figure 3). Quote it exactly that way.
- The adjusted student-level profile of who moves, as description: conditional on everything else in the model, Black students (+2.2 pp), students experiencing homelessness (+7.6 pp), students with disabilities (+1.4 pp) and older students remain more mobile (Table 8, Col. A), and these student-block coefficients are stable across the Table A3 ladder.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "The first large-scale longitudinal analysis of school mobility among students in foster care" (p.11; "first large-scale analysis ... in California," p.2) — Barrat and Berliner (2013) established the one-third rate and the alternative-school pattern with the same linkage, Barrat et al. (2025) report a decade of stability trends, and Clemens et al. (2017) is a statewide longitudinal study with actual placement records. Cite this paper for the 2017–24 series and the new exhibits, not for opening the question.
- "Students typically relocate more than 20 miles" (abstract) and "on average ... 22.5 miles" (pp.6–7, 12) — the number is a median, not a mean; it is computed only over residential moves that changed ZIP code, so it excludes the shortest moves by construction; it is measured ZIP-to-ZIP, not home-to-school-of-origin; and California's child-welfare indicators (CCWIP) report roughly half of children in care living within five miles of the removal home, a different quantity the paper does not mention. "This is the first study to examine how far students in foster care move" (p.4) is true of the measure, not the question.
- "Residential moves ... serving as a major driver" (abstract) and the 44.99 pp effect (p.11) — a contemporaneous correlation whose sequence the authors say they cannot establish (p.5), estimated from a field that may be refreshed mainly when a new enrollment record is created. It restates the two-thirds co-occurrence; it is not evidence about mechanism or magnitude.
- "Some community factors, such as child poverty [and housing affordability], became more relevant after the pandemic" (abstract, p.3) — the poverty interaction replicates across Table 9 and Table A6, which is in its favor, but rests on student-clustered standard errors for a district-level regressor and on a mechanism (the Child Tax Credit expiry) that the SAIPE measure would not register; the affordability estimate is largest during, not after, the pandemic (Table 9: .0037 vs .0024), is positive in sign, and reverses without Los Angeles (Table A3).
- "Future efforts ... should also focus on ... improving housing affordability" (p.13) — the paper's own estimate says more affordable counties have more mobility (+.0013 per index point, p.11; Table 8). Do not cite the paper as evidence that affordability reduces foster-youth school mobility.
- "Most of the estimates are consistent across specifications" (p.9) — true for the student block, false for the school and community blocks (Table A3 sign flips on HAI, facilities, school % multilingual, school % low-income, town district). Read any school- or community-level coefficient from Table A3, including the "w/o LA" column, before quoting it.
- "[Residence change, disability, homelessness and alternative-setting enrollment] remain significant in all three time periods, and this is true across most racial/ethnic groups (Table A4) and age/grade groups (Table A5)" (p.11) — holds for residential change and, except for Asian students, homelessness; disability is significant in all three periods only for Black students and is n.s. for middle/high school post-COVID (.0039); alternative-setting enrollment is significant in all three periods only for Latino students and in neither grade band.
- The decline "may be attributed to" Family First (2018), the Continuum of Care Reform (2015) and school-of-origin outreach (p.11) — the level is flat across the two pre-pandemic years, the drop coincides with distance learning, the in-care population fell 22% (note 3), reduced maltreatment reporting during closures is a documented alternative, and nothing in the paper tests any of these. Treat the trend as descriptive.
- "In some cases, students move to better-resourced schools" (abstract; 30% high-poverty to affluent, 15% high-need to low-need, Table 7) — "affluent" and "low-need" are never defined, the denominator is all school changers rather than those starting in high-poverty schools, and the reverse flow is not reported, so the net direction is unknown.
- Interview-based explanations — rural placement and transportation shortages, schools with more students with disabilities providing transportation (p.11) — come from one question in seven counties that the paper itself says are not standalone findings (p.4); the coefficients they explain are not stable across periods (rural is significant only pre-COVID, Table 9).
- Numbers that appear only in the prose — the 6%/7%/8%/16% comparison rates (p.5), the 35% and 23% between-year figures (p.4), the 38% vs 60% graduation rates for alternative vs traditional settings (p.11), and "most students in foster care attended high-poverty schools" (p.7) — have no supporting exhibit; cite them as the authors' statements.
- Any count derived from the Ns in Tables 5, 6 or A2, or from the three-year rates in Table 3/A1 — the units and windows are not stated and cannot be reconciled with Table 4 from what is printed.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is a descriptive study built on unusually strong data: statewide California enrollment records linked to child-welfare records for every student in foster care from 2017–18 to 2023–24. The headline descriptive facts (about 31% midyear mobility, higher rates for Black, high school, and homeless students, a decline from about 36% to 30%, and residential moves with median distances above 20 miles) are credible, allowing for a few measurement caveats. The regression layer (RQ4) is weaker, and readers should put much less weight on it. It conditions on a co-determined "residential change" variable. It clusters standard errors only at the student level while its community variables vary at the district and county level. It silently drops a third of student-years. Several of its school and community coefficients change sign across specifications. That includes the housing-affordability result featured in the abstract and the discussion, whose policy reading also runs against the estimated sign.

**Strengths:**

- **Population-scale administrative data.** The analysis covers essentially the full population of California students in foster care: 133,127 students, with yearly enrollment falling from 49,983 in 2017–18 to 39,099 in 2023–24 (p.3, Data Sources; Table 1). Foster status comes from a statewide CDE–CDSS record match with a stated match rate of about 94% (p.3), which is more credible than school-reported flags or survey self-reports.
- **A defensible outcome, clearly motivated.** The paper studies within-year (midyear) mobility and explains why (p.4). It reports how much the figure rises when between-year moves are counted (31% to 35%). The appendix spells out the counting rules: primary enrollments only, stays of 5 days or fewer excluded (about 175 students), and dropouts, suspensions, summer moves, and dual enrollment not counted as moves (p.16).
- **Disaggregation that serves readers.** Mobility is broken out by race, grade band, and need category (Table 3, p.6), by number of moves and destination (Table 4, p.6; Table A2, p.16), by school type (Table 6, p.7), and by year (Figure 1, p.8; Table A1, p.16). Readers can see the heterogeneity directly instead of only through regression coefficients.
- **A new measure: residential travel distance.** Zip-to-zip distances between successive residences (Table 5, p.6; Figure 3, p.9) are new to this literature. The authors are candid that the measure is limited: they cannot tell whether the school move or the home move came first, within-zip moves are missed, and reunification moves cannot be identified (pp.4–5).
- **A transparent specification ladder.** Table A3 (p.17) adds covariate blocks one at a time, then county fixed effects, then drops Los Angeles County. Readers can see how estimates move, and that transparency is what makes several of the fragility findings below visible.
- **Honest scoping of the qualitative component.** The authors say the interviews are not stand-alone findings and were used only to guide specification and interpretation (p.4).

**Weaknesses:**

- **The residential-change control is a "bad control" and a near-mechanical correlate.** Residential change and school change are jointly produced by the same event, a placement change, and the paper cannot establish which came first (p.5). Its marginal effect is .4499 (p.10, Table 8, Col. A). Every other coefficient in the preferred model is therefore a "net of moving home" association, which understates total disparities. Homelessness is the clearest case: its marginal effect falls from .1783 without the residence control to .0674 with it (p.17, Table A3, Base vs. Base w/zip). The Black coefficient falls from .0441 to .0281. The same Table A3 step also changes the sample (304,466 to 279,154 observations), so part of each drop may reflect the sample rather than the control.
- **Standard errors are clustered too finely for the community-level claims (checkable: Table 8 note, p.10; Table A3 note, p.17).** Standard errors are clustered at the student level only. Yet district poverty, city crime, the county housing-affordability index (HAI), county facility counts, and county STRTP shares vary only at the district-year or county-year level. With county fixed effects, the county-level variables are identified from about 58 counties x 7 years of within-county change. Student-level clustering almost certainly overstates the precision of those estimates (for example, the HAI standard error of .0002, p.10). The significance stars on community factors should not be taken at face value.
- **About a third of the sample disappears without explanation (checkable: p.17, Table A3).** Observations fall from 304,466 (Base) to 279,154 (with zip), 251,073 (with school), 203,125 (with community), and 203,095 (preferred model, which is also Table 8 Col. A). That is about 33% of student-years. The largest single drop (about 48,000) comes when community variables are added. The paper never mentions this complete-case loss, reports no mobility rate for the regression sample, and does not compare dropped with retained observations. Because each column of Table A3 uses a different sample, coefficient changes across columns mix changes in specification with changes in sample.
- **School and community coefficients are unstable across specifications (checkable: p.17, Table A3).** The text says "most of the estimates are consistent across specifications" (p.9). That holds for student characteristics, not for the school and community variables:
  - HAI is .0021** (w/ Comm), .0013** (w/ Co FE), and −.0021** (w/o LA). The sign flips when Los Angeles is excluded.
  - Total foster care facilities is .0095** without county fixed effects and −.0387** with them.
  - School % multilingual learners is −.0319**, then .0305**.
  - School % low-income is .0371**, then −.0001, then .0220** (w/o LA).
  - Dropping Los Angeles removes 60,831 of 203,095 observations (about 30%).
- **The housing-affordability interpretation contradicts the estimated sign.** HAI is defined as the share of households that can afford a median-priced home (p.11), so higher values mean more affordable housing. The preferred estimate is positive (.0013**, p.10, Table 8, Col. A), and the post-COVID interaction is also positive (.0014**, p.19, Table A6). Taken at face value, more affordable counties or years have more mobility. Yet the discussion concludes that efforts to reduce mobility "should also focus on ... improving housing affordability" (p.13). The recommendation does not follow from the estimate. The estimate itself also reverses sign without Los Angeles (above).
- **Several coefficients cannot be interpreted as reported.** Units are not given for the share variables (child poverty, school % SWD, % highly mobile) or for facility counts. The text reads the poverty coefficient as a "5.00 pp increase in school mobility" (p.11) without saying per what change. If poverty is a 0–1 proportion, .0500 corresponds to moving from 0% to 100% poverty. District enrollment and crime are reported as .0000 (.0000) with significance stars (p.10, Table 8).
- **Estimates labeled as "effects" are associations.** Table 8 is titled "Effects of Student, School, and Community Characteristics," and the text uses "driver" and "increases the probability" (pp.9–11). Nothing in the design identifies causal effects. The paper is descriptive, and its regression should be read that way.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Rely on the descriptive statistics in Tables 3–5 and Figure 1.** These are the paper's most dependable contributions: 31% midyear mobility, the group gradients, the roughly two-thirds co-occurrence with residential change, and median residential moves of 20–30 miles. Keep in mind that "in foster care" means in care on any day of the year (p.3), so some counted moves happen before entry or after exit.
- **Use the right table for total gaps.** For the size of the Black, homelessness, or disability gaps, use Table 3 (p.6) or the Base column of Table A3 (p.17), not Table 8. Table 8's student coefficients are conditional on a residential move and understate total disparities.
- **Treat the school and community coefficients in Table 8 as fragile descriptions.** This covers HAI, facilities, STRTP share, school composition, and crime. They are not risk factors. Their signs depend on county fixed effects and on whether Los Angeles is included (Table A3), and their standard errors are understated.
- **Do not cite this paper as evidence that improving housing affordability would reduce school mobility.** The estimated sign points the other way and is not robust (p.10, Table 8; p.17, Table A3, w/o LA).
- **Treat the post-pandemic poverty finding as suggestive only.** It appears in both the split-sample models (−.0505 pre-COVID vs. .2070** post-COVID; p.12, Table 9) and the interaction model (.1745**; p.19, Table A6), which is a point in its favor. It still rests on student-clustered standard errors and on a district poverty measure that, as far as can be judged, would not register the Child Tax Credit changes the discussion uses to explain it (p.13).
- **Read the "rural districts" story as a pre-pandemic pattern.** Rural mobility is higher by 2.13 pp in the pooled model (p.10, Table 8), but the difference is significant only before COVID (.0389**) and not during (.0165) or after (.0117) (p.12, Table 9).
- **Read the 36% to 30% decline as a descriptive trend, not a policy effect.** The foster population shrank 22% over the period (note 3, p.13), so its composition may have changed. The attribution to Family First and Continuum of Care Reform (p.11) is conjecture that no analysis in the paper tests.
- **Do not read the zip-code distances as commute distances to the school of origin.** They measure distance between successive residences, only when the zip code changed (pp.4–5). They are an indirect signal of how hard it would be to stay in the same school.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Design and what it can support.* The paper answers four questions, three purely descriptive (RQ1–RQ3) and one correlational (RQ4). For RQ1–RQ3 the design fits: a near-census of the target population in linked administrative records, with a clearly defined outcome. The main threats are measurement, not identification. For RQ4, Equation (1) (p.5) is a pooled probit of a student-year mobility indicator on student, start-of-year school, district, and community covariates, with year fixed effects and, in the preferred model, county fixed effects. No identifying assumption is stated because no causal effect is being identified. The problem is that the reporting slides into causal language: the Table 8 title (p.10), residential change as a "primary driver" (p.9), and the policy recommendations built on community coefficients (p.13). The design can describe how mobility varies with these characteristics among foster students. It cannot say that changing any of them would change mobility.

*The residential-change variable.* This is the most consequential specification choice. A placement change typically causes both a new address and a new school, and the authors state they "cannot determine whether a school change happened before or after they moved" (p.5). A 45 pp marginal effect (p.10, Table 8) mostly restates that these two events are the same event seen through two data fields. Including it does two things. First, it absorbs much of the variation that runs through placement instability. That is why the homelessness coefficient falls by more than 60% and the Black coefficient by about a third when it enters (p.17, Table A3, Base to Base w/zip). Second, it makes the remaining coefficients "direct" associations, net of moving home, which is seldom the quantity a reader or policymaker wants. The linked evidence is also imperfect: within-zip moves are missed, and zip changes are not always placement changes (p.5). The "67% of school moves were accompanied by a change in student residence" figure (p.5; Table 3, Col. B, p.6) has no benchmark against non-movers in the text. Only the regression coefficient shows that residential change is far more common among school movers.

*Inference.* Student-level clustering (notes to Tables 8, 9, A3–A6) handles repeated observations of the same student, but not correlation among students who share a district-year or county-year. Moulton-type understatement of standard errors is well documented for exactly this setup: a group-level regressor combined with individual-level clustering. It is especially serious with county fixed effects, because the county-level regressors then vary only over time within 58 counties. The split-sample estimates in Table 9 (p.12) show the practical cost. The "total number of foster care facilities" coefficient is −.0385 pre-COVID, −.2145 during COVID, and −.0435 post-COVID. The COVID figure is estimated from roughly two years of within-county change. Yet the interaction model finds essentially no period difference for facilities (.0001 and −.0001; p.19, Table A6). Estimates this unstable, reported with student-clustered standard errors near .01 to .02, are a warning sign. Separately, in a probit the marginal effect of an interaction term is not a single, simply defined number. The paper does not explain how the "marginal effects" of interactions in Table A6 were computed, so readers should interpret those entries cautiously.

*Sample construction and consistency of counts.* Several counts need clarification before anyone builds on them:

- **Units in Table 1 (p.3).** The foster column reports 133,127 students. The "All Students" column reports 43,223,355, which is roughly seven years of statewide enrollment and so appears to count student-years. The two columns may not use the same unit. (This is inferred from magnitudes; the paper does not say.)
- **The regression sample.** Base observations (304,466; p.17, Table A3) match the number of foster student-years, so the analysis unit is the student-year. The preferred model keeps 203,095 of them (Table 8, p.10) with no account of the losses.
- **Repeated Ns (checkable).** The same student counts, 49,913, 20,316, and 9,041, appear in Table 5 (p.6), Table 6 (p.7), and Table A2 (p.16). Table 5 is about residential moves; Tables 6 and A2 are about school moves. The paper does not say whether Table 5 is restricted to school movers, and without that the identical Ns are hard to interpret.
- **The ratios behind those Ns do not match Table 4.** 20,316/49,913 is about 41% with a second move, versus (7%+3%)/31%, about 32%, implied by Table 4 (p.6). This may reflect pooling across years (unique students vs. student-years), but the unit is never stated.
- **Destination categories (Table 4, p.6).** Same district 9%, different district 16%, and different county 12% do not sum to the 31% mover rate under any obvious nesting. It is not stated whether they are mutually exclusive.
- **A possible artifact in "different district."** Juvenile court and county community schools are run by county offices of education (p.7). If those offices carry their own district codes, as California school codes appear to assign them, a move from a local school into a county-run juvenile court school would count as "moving to a different district" even with no geographic move. That would inflate the cross-district share the paper reads as evidence of long-distance placement. This could not be verified from the paper.
- **The three-year mobility window.** Table A1 (p.16) reports three-year mobility for every year from 2017–18 through 2023–24, but the data span only those years. The paper does not define the window. It is unclear how the 2017–18 or 2023–24 values were computed, and the 2023–24 low (44%) may partly reflect truncation.
- **Between-year comparison (p.4).** Foster students' mobility rises only from 31% to 35% when between-year moves are added, while 23% of the general population moves between years. The foster figure excludes structural moves; the paper does not say whether the general-population figure does. The comparison may not be like-for-like.

*Measurement of mobility and school type.* Counting juvenile court school enrollment as a school move is defensible from an educational-disruption standpoint, but readers should see what it implies. A detention-and-release sequence (traditional to juvenile court to traditional) produces two "moves." That mechanically raises the multiple-move counts and the share of alternative settings in later moves (p.7, Table 6: alternative-to-alternative rises from 7% to 18% by the third move). It also partly explains the 3.30 pp coefficient on starting the year in an alternative setting (p.10, Table 8). The "better-resourced school" statistics (p.8, Table 7) report only upward moves (30% of movers going from high-poverty to "affluent" schools), with no definition of "affluent" and no count of downward moves. They cannot tell a reader whether mobility systematically improves or worsens school resources.

*Trends and the pandemic.* The descriptive trend is faithfully described. Figure 1 (p.8) shows about 36% in both pre-pandemic years, a trough near 23% in 2020–21, and about 30% by 2023–24. The share moving more than once goes from about 14% to about 10%, matching the text. Two cautions apply.

- **Composition.** The in-care population fell by 22% (note 3, p.13). If prevention policy kept lower-risk children out of care, or changed how many children enter care midyear (an entry itself often forces a school move), the trend would partly reflect who is counted rather than stability for a given child. The paper does not report composition-adjusted year effects, which would be the natural check.
- **Small gap changes.** The Black–White gap "decreased ... from 7% in 2017–18 to 5% in 2023–24" (p.8). Figure 2 (p.9) shows 7, 6, 6, −1, 6, 5, and about 5 across the years, with no uncertainty shown. That is closer to a stable gap with a pandemic anomaly than to a clear narrowing.
- **Inconsistent distance-trend text.** The text on distance trends is also slightly inconsistent. Page 7 says the median distance "has risen over time." Page 8 says it "has decreased in recent years, particularly for the first and second residence moves." Figure 3 (p.9) supports both readings depending on the baseline: first-move medians rise from about 21 to about 24 miles in 2020–21 and then ease to about 23. Only the third-move series rises clearly, to 35 miles in 2023–24.

*The community-factor conclusions.* The abstract's claim that "some community factors, such as child poverty, became more relevant after the pandemic" (p.1) is the paper's most policy-salient regression result. It is also its most fragile.

- **Child poverty.** This finding does replicate across the split-sample (p.12, Table 9) and interaction (p.19, Table A6) approaches, which is to the paper's credit. Against that, district child poverty (Census SAIPE, per the Table 8 source note) is a modeled estimate. With county fixed effects, its year-to-year variation within a county is thin and plausibly noisy, and the student-level standard errors overstate precision. The discussion's mechanism, the post-2021 expiration of the expanded Child Tax Credit and a near-tripling of child poverty (p.13), also sits poorly with the variable. SAIPE-type estimates target official money-income poverty, which to my understanding does not count tax credits, so the measured variable may not track the mechanism offered.
- **Housing affordability.** As noted above, the direction the paper draws from the result is the opposite of the estimated sign, and the pooled estimate reverses when Los Angeles is excluded (p.17, Table A3).

*Qualitative component.* The interviews (over 50 in seven counties, spring 2025, one question analyzed; p.4) are appropriately scoped. In practice, though, they mainly supply after-the-fact explanations for coefficients: for the rural effect, and for the negative coefficient on a school's share of students with disabilities (p.11). Both of those estimates are unstable across periods (p.12, Table 9: the school SWD share is not significant during COVID, and the rural effect is not significant after 2019). Readers should treat these explanations as plausible stories, not corroboration.

*Reproducibility.* The data are FERPA-restricted. The authors point to CDE's research data request process and offer do-files to approved users (p.13). That is a reasonable arrangement for restricted data, but outside readers cannot check the sample-construction questions raised above.

*Bottom line.* As a descriptive portrait of midyear school mobility among California foster youth, the paper is solid and useful. The main rates, group differences, co-occurrence with residential moves, the long residential distances, and the pandemic dip and partial recovery are all well supported. As an account of which school and community factors "affect" mobility, it is not reliable. Its student-level coefficients are conditional on a co-determined variable. Its community-level inference is overstated, its estimation sample is unexplained, and several of its community coefficients, including housing affordability, are not robust in sign. The overall rating is Adequate because the paper's central, descriptive contribution holds up. Much of the RQ4 material, taken alone, would rate lower.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper's account of the policy background is clear and useful: federal and California educational-stability law, school-of-origin rules, and the Continuum of Care Reform. Its account of the research record is thin, though, and in places inaccurate. It leaves out the most direct California antecedent, Barrat and Berliner's 2013 statewide "Invisible Achievement Gap" report. That report used the same CALPADS–CWS/CMS linkage and had already documented a one-third within-year mobility rate and heavy enrollment in nontraditional schools. The paper also does not use the 2025 WestEd follow-up it cites, which reports school-stability trends from 2014 to 2023. As a result, its "first large-scale longitudinal analysis" claims are overstated. Several citations are mischaracterized or garbled in the reference list, and the paper hardly engages with the economics and child-welfare work that complicates its framing. Readers can use the paper as a solid descriptive update covering the COVID era. They should not use its literature review as a map of the field.

**Strengths:**

- The policy context is thorough and accurate enough to be useful on its own: the Fostering Connections Act (2008), ESSA's school-of-origin and transportation provisions, the 2016 and 2024 ED/HHS non-regulatory guidance, California's Continuum of Care Reform, the 2021 CDE–CDSS joint best-interest guidance, and California Education Code 48853.5's broader definition of "school of origin" (pp. 2–3). A reader new to the topic gets a clear picture of the institutional setting the data come from.
- The paper grounds its main mechanism, placement-driven residential moves, in the closest empirical antecedent, Clemens et al. (2017). It characterizes that study accurately (checkable): the paper says 31% of initial removals and more than 40% of subsequent placement changes produced a school move (p. 5). Clemens et al.'s Table 3 reports 31% for first removals and 40–52% for the various transition types. The paper's "roughly two-thirds of school moves accompany a residence change" (p. 2; p. 5, Table 3 Col. B, 67%) also lines up in magnitude with Clemens et al.'s finding that about two-thirds of school moves fall under educational-stability protections.
- The general school-mobility literature is cited from reasonable anchor sources: the Mehana and Reynolds (2004) meta-analysis, Reynolds et al. (2009), Welsh's (2017) *Review of Educational Research* synthesis, Grigg (2012), and Langenkamp (2016). Grigg is a fair citation for the claim that midyear moves are especially disruptive (p. 2). In his Nashville data, compulsory moves during the school year carried much larger achievement penalties than other move types.
- The paper labels its qualitative component honestly (p. 4). The interviews are used to inform specification and interpretation rather than presented as findings, and the thematic-analysis method is cited (Braun & Clarke, 2021).
- The paper cites the dual-system-youth replication by Herz et al. (2021) to explain the overlap between foster care and juvenile court schools (p. 11, note 8). That is the right literature for the alternative-setting finding.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The closest California predecessor is missing (checkable: absent from the reference list, pp. 14–15).** Barrat and Berliner (2013, WestEd), *The Invisible Achievement Gap, Part 1*, linked CALPADS with CWS/CMS for about 43,000 students in foster care in 2009–10. It reported that "one third of students in foster care changed schools at least once during the school year." It also reported that just under 10% attended three or more schools in a year, and that students in foster care were more likely to attend nontraditional public schools. Those are the paper's RQ1 headline (31%, p. 5) and part of RQ2, established more than a decade earlier with the same data infrastructure. Frerer et al. (2013), another California study, is also absent; Clemens et al. (2017) cite it for foster-youth transfer rates two to three times those of peers.
- **The novelty claims are overstated, and one is contradicted by a source the paper cites.** The paper says "few longitudinal studies have investigated how school mobility patterns change over time" and claims "the first large-scale analysis of school mobility trends ... in California" (p. 2). The Discussion goes further and drops the California qualifier: "the first large-scale longitudinal analysis of school mobility among students in foster care" (p. 11). But Barrat et al. (2025), which the paper cites only once, for outcome gaps (p. 1), is subtitled "Trends in Education Outcomes of Students in Foster Care." According to WestEd's public summary, it analyzes 2014–2023 and reports that the share of foster youth enrolled at only one school per year rose over the decade. Outside California, Clemens et al. (2017) followed all Colorado students first removed from home between 2010 and 2015 (N = 6,405) in statewide linked longitudinal data. Clemens et al. (2016, *Children and Youth Services Review* 68) tracked four statewide high-school cohorts. Neither 2016 paper nor the 2025 report is engaged on this point.
- **The claim to be the first study of distance is too broad.** The paper states: "this is the first study to examine how far students in foster care move" (p. 4). The UC Berkeley California Child Welfare Indicators Project (CCWIP) has long reported placement distance from the home address for California children in care, republished on kidsdata.org. In 2013, 38% of children still in care after one year lived 11 or more miles from home, and about 48% lived within five miles. The paper's measure is new: ZIP-to-ZIP distances between successive residential ZIP codes in education records. The question it answers is not.
- **Several citations are mischaracterized or bibliographically garbled (checkable against the reference list).**
  - *Hanushek et al. (2004)* is cited for the claim that moves during the school year "have greater impacts on student learning" (p. 4). HKR report that for movers themselves, "the hypothesis that the timing of the move (i.e. moving during the school year) has no effect on the cost of moving cannot be rejected" (HKR 2004, p. 1736). Their midyear finding is about the externality on non-movers in high-turnover schools.
  - *Cutuli et al. (2013)* is cited for foster-care students' dropout, discipline, and proficiency gaps (p. 1). It is a Minneapolis study of homeless and highly mobile students and does not isolate foster care.
  - *Kemp & Bodonyi (2000)* is listed as "Foster care dynamics 1983–1998: A report from the multistate foster care archive. Chapin Hall" (p. 15). The Chapin Hall *Foster Care Dynamics* series is authored by Wulczyn and colleagues. Kemp and Bodonyi (2000) is a *Child and Family Social Work* article about infants in foster care, which is an odd source for the claim about older children's placement difficulties (p. 5). The entry appears to merge two sources.
  - *Gustavsson & MacEachron (2012)* is listed as *Children and Youth Services Review* 34(12), but its DOI (10.1093/cs/cds005) resolves to *Children & Schools* 34(2), 83–91. It is also a policy review, not the empirical evidence of higher mobility rates it is cited for (p. 1).
  - The Clemens et al. (2017) DOI in the reference list (…2017.10.031) does not match the article's DOI (…2017.11.003).
  - "Brueckner et al., 2021" in the text (p. 13) is dated 2023 in the reference list.
- **The paper barely engages conflicting or complicating evidence.** The introduction presents school moves as uniformly harmful and cumulative (pp. 1–2). The fuller evidence base is more mixed. Welsh (2017), whom the paper cites, stresses that mobility effects shrink substantially once selection is addressed. HKR (2004) find average disruption costs of a few hundredths of a standard deviation, partly offset by school-quality gains for district switchers. Schwartz, Stiefel, and Cordes (2017, *Education Finance and Policy*) use NYC data and instruments to separate causal effects from selection. Pears et al. (2015), cited three times, found that early school moves predicted poorer socioemotional competence only among children with weaker early learning skills. On foster care itself, the quasi-experimental economics literature is absent: Doyle (2007, *American Economic Review*); Gross and Baron (2022, *AEJ: Applied*), who found that placement *raised* Michigan children's attendance and math scores; and Bald et al. (2022, *Journal of Economic Perspectives*). That literature bears directly on how readers should read the "foster care causes poor outcomes" framing (p. 1).
- **The COVID-era and trend explanations rely on general-population or popular sources and skip the child-welfare-specific evidence.** The post-pandemic housing mechanism is supported by work on work-from-home migration and the "donut effect" (Brueckner et al.; Ramani & Bloom, p. 13). Shortage of placements is supported by an LA Times article and an NPR segment (p. 6). The mobility decline is attributed to Family First and CCR without any evaluation evidence (p. 11). The paper does not cite work showing that pandemic school closures sharply cut maltreatment reporting (Baron, Goldstein & Wallace, 2020, *Journal of Public Economics*). Fewer reports mean fewer new removals and fewer removal-triggered school moves, which is a plausible, literature-grounded alternative explanation for the 2019–20/2020–21 dip. The paper also does not discuss how declining caseloads change the composition of the foster-care population (note 3 reports a 22% enrollment decline, p. 13).
- **The reference base is narrow for a paper of this scope.** By my count, the reference list has about 50 entries (checkable, pp. 14–15), of which roughly 19–20 are peer-reviewed journal articles. The rest are statutes, government web pages, reports, two blogs (including a PPIC blog co-authored by the lead author, used as the sole source for California reopening dates), a newspaper article, and a radio segment.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **For the "one in three foster youth change schools midyear" fact, cite Barrat & Berliner (2013) as the original California source.** Cite this paper for the 2017–18 to 2023–24 update (36% to 30%, p. 3 and Figure 1, p. 8). Do not splice the 2009–10 and 2017–24 numbers into a single trend without checking that the definitions match. Barrat and Berliner used a statewide matched snapshot, while this paper counts anyone in care at any point in the year (p. 3). CDE also publishes a differently defined "stability rate" for foster youth on DataQuest.
- **For trends over time, read Barrat et al. (2025) alongside this paper.** It covers 2014–2023 with the same state systems and reports improving stability. Treat this paper's "first longitudinal" claims (pp. 2, 11) as unsupported.
- **For the mechanism linking placements and school moves, Clemens et al. (2017) is the more detailed source.** It observes actual placement dates and types, which this paper cannot (p. 5). It shows that reunification ends in a school move 35% of the time and that school moves cluster in the year before removal. Both findings matter here because the paper counts mobility for anyone in care "at any point during a school year" (p. 3). Some of the moves it counts may therefore precede entry into care or follow exit from it.
- **Read the distance finding against CCWIP's placement-proximity indicators.** CCWIP data show roughly half of California children in care after a year living within five miles of their removal home. This paper's median of more than 22 miles (p. 8, Table 5) is conditional on a ZIP-code change, so it leaves out short moves by construction (the paper acknowledges this, p. 5). The two figures describe different things, and the ">20 miles" headline in the abstract should not be read as the typical placement distance.
- **Check citations before repeating them.** Do not cite HKR (2004) for "midyear moves hurt movers more," Cutuli et al. (2013) for foster-care outcomes, or the "Kemp & Bodonyi (2000)" Chapin Hall entry without checking the originals.
- **For the "moves to better-resourced schools" result (p. 8, Table 7), the relevant frame is HKR's disruption-versus-Tiebout distinction.** In that study, measured school-quality gains were concentrated among within-region district switchers and were small and insignificant for Black students (HKR 2004, p. 1736). Also relevant is Rumberger's distinction between strategic and reactive moves (Rumberger, 2003; 2015 NEPC brief). Table 7 is descriptive and says nothing about whether such moves help.
- **Useful companion readings on causal effects:** Gross and Baron (2022) and Bald et al. (2022) on the effects of foster care; Schwartz, Stiefel, and Cordes (2017) and Welsh (2017) on the effects of school mobility; Min (2022, *Education and Urban Society*) on between-year versus within-year mobility.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What the paper can be cited for.* After correcting for the omissions below, the paper's real contributions are narrower than its framing but still worth having:

- a seven-year, statewide series (2017–18 to 2023–24) that spans the pandemic;
- a ZIP-based distance measure built from education records;
- a move-order breakdown of transitions into alternative settings, showing that traditional-to-traditional moves fall from 72% of first moves to 54% of third-or-later moves (p. 8, Table 6);
- a descriptive regression that links community covariates (child poverty, county housing affordability, foster-facility counts) to mobility (p. 10, Table 8).

None of these, as far as I can determine, appeared together in earlier California work. They are the right reasons to cite the paper. What readers should not take from it is its account of what came before it.

*The missing California lineage.* The most consequential omission is Barrat and Berliner (2013), because this paper is in effect a successor to it. Both use the CDE–CDSS statewide match. Both measure within-year mobility. Both find about a third of students in foster care changing schools during the year (Barrat & Berliner: 68% stayed in one school all year; this paper: 31%, p. 5). Both find disproportionate enrollment in nontraditional schools (compare this paper's Table 1, p. 3). Barrat and Berliner also reported that just under 10% of students in foster care attended three or more schools in a year. This paper's Table 4 (p. 6) reports the share moving three or more times; readers can compare the two directly. The paper does cite the 2025 WestEd follow-up (Barrat et al., 2025), but only as evidence that foster youth have worse outcomes (p. 1). That report's own summary describes a decade of trend analysis in which school stability improved. The paper's trend finding is therefore corroboration of that report's finding, not a first. Framed that way, the COVID-era detail would have been more convincing, because two independent teams using the same systems reach consistent conclusions. The paper also never mentions CCWIP, the long-running UC Berkeley/CDSS child-welfare indicator system. CCWIP is the natural source for California placement-stability and placement-proximity benchmarks. The paper instead reaches for a national Kids Count figure and a Children's Bureau outcome table (p. 5), and I could not verify the exact denominators behind those two statistics.

*Novelty claims, claim by claim.*

- (a) "Few longitudinal studies" of change over time (p. 2): overstated. See Clemens et al. (2017) for Colorado 2010–2015, and Barrat et al. (2025) for California 2014–2023.
- (b) "Limited knowledge about the distances" (p. 2) and "first study to examine how far students in foster care move" (p. 4): true only for this specific measure. California's child-welfare indicators have reported placement distance from home for years.
- (c) "Little is known about the types of schools they move to or from" (p. 2): partly fair. Earlier work documented *where foster youth are enrolled*. The *transition-by-move-order* analysis in Table 6 does appear new.
- (d) "Comprehensive large-scale studies examining how student, family, and community factors interact ... are scarce" (p. 2): fair for foster youth specifically, though the regression includes no interactions among those factors except community-by-period terms (Table A6, p. 19). A growing general-population literature models transfer risk across student, school, and neighborhood levels. Terada et al. (2025, *Education and Urban Society*) is one recent example; I have not read it closely enough to characterize its findings.

*Characterization problems a reader could propagate.* The HKR (2004) citation matters most, because the paper uses it to justify its main design choice: focusing on within-year rather than between-year mobility (p. 4). HKR explicitly tested move timing and could not reject that midyear moves cost movers no more than moves before the school year. What they did find is that midyear *entrants* impose larger costs on their classmates. That is a real reason to care about midyear moves, but it is not the one the paper gives. Grigg (2012) does support the paper's claim, so the design choice is defensible; the citation is simply wrong for it. The other problems are smaller but add up:

- A homeless/highly-mobile-student study (Cutuli et al., 2013) is presented as foster-care evidence.
- A Chapin Hall report appears under the wrong authors.
- Two DOIs and one journal name do not match the articles.
- A policy commentary (Gustavsson & MacEachron) is cited as evidence that research "consistently shows" higher mobility.
- Clemens et al. (2017) and Kennedy et al. (2023, a meta-regression of racial disparities in foster-youth wellbeing) are cited together as evidence that school moves contribute to later employment and justice-system outcomes (p. 1). Neither directly tests that pathway.

Readers who build on this paper should trace these claims back to their primary sources.

*Conflicting evidence and adjacent fields.* In economics, the paper cites HKR only for timing and ignores its central point: some mobility is quality-seeking. That point bears directly on the paper's own finding that about 30% of school changers moved from high-poverty to more affluent schools (p. 8, Table 7). Economics is also where the credible causal evidence on foster care now lives: judge/investigator-assignment designs (Doyle, 2007; Gross & Baron, 2022). Gross and Baron found *positive* educational effects of placement for marginal cases in Michigan. That does not contradict anything the paper estimates, but it undercuts the introduction's implicit causal story that foster care plus mobility produce poor outcomes (p. 1).

From developmental psychology, Pears et al. (2015) is cited three times as general evidence of harm. The study's own findings are conditional: effects appear on socioemotional competence, and only for children with weaker early learning skills, in a sample of 86 children in foster care. From child-welfare research, Oosterman et al. (2007) is used appropriately for age-related placement disruption (p. 5). But the California-specific placement-stability literature is not engaged. An example is Webster, Barth, and Needell (2000, *Child Welfare*), a longitudinal analysis of placement stability using California data. From sociology and housing research, the paper cites national work-from-home migration papers for a post-pandemic housing mechanism (p. 13). It does not engage with work on residential instability among low-income families, or with the 2020–21 eviction moratoria. Those moratoria are a more direct candidate explanation for the drop in residential changes from about 30% to 23% (p. 7) than the "emergency restrictions" the paper offers.

Two citation-to-evidence mismatches in the Discussion deserve a reader's attention. First, the paper cites the Annie E. Casey Foundation's finding that child poverty "nearly tripled to 13% between 2021 and 2024" (p. 13). To my knowledge, that figure refers to the national Supplemental Poverty Measure. The paper's regressors come from Census SAIPE (Table 8 source note, p. 10), which uses the official poverty measure. So the cited trend is not a trend in the variable being modeled. Second, the paper recommends "improving housing affordability" (p. 13), supported by housing-market literature. But the paper's own estimate is that a *more* affordable county (higher HAI) is associated with *higher* mobility: .0013 in Table 8, Col. A, p. 10, described on p. 11 as a .13 pp increase per point of HAI. The positive HAI × post-COVID interaction (.0014, Table A6, p. 19) points the same way. That may have a sensible explanation, for example that affordable counties are more rural or have fewer placement options. But the cited literature does not provide it, and readers should not treat the housing recommendation as grounded in the paper's evidence.

*Qualitative traditions.* The paper's qualitative component (p. 4) could have drawn on existing qualitative and mixed-methods work on educational stability. Examples include youth-voice studies such as Clemens, Helm, Myers, Thomas, and Tis (2017, *Children and Youth Services Review*) and the interview component of Barrat et al. (2025). Citing that work would show whether the themes from seven counties (placement shortages, transportation, rural barriers) replicate earlier findings or are new. As written, those themes rest on the paper's own interviews plus journalism (p. 6).

*Calibration note.* My knowledge of California foster-youth reports and of the child-welfare indicator literature is incomplete. I verified the key omissions and mischaracterizations above against the primary documents or their publishers' pages: the Barrat & Berliner 2013 report text, the Clemens et al. 2017 article text, the HKR 2004 article text, and the WestEd 2025 summary. I did not read the full 2025 WestEd report, and I have not verified the Kids Count and Children's Bureau denominators. There may be additional relevant California studies I have missed, which would strengthen rather than weaken the conclusion that the paper's novelty claims are overstated.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper is short, clearly signposted by research question, and its headline descriptive numbers (the 31% pooled mobility rate, the 36%-to-30% decline, the group gaps in Table 3) are reported faithfully in the text and abstract. The problems are in the regression narrative and the discussion. Several summary sentences say more than the appendix tables show, one policy recommendation runs against the sign of the paper's own estimate, and a number of exhibits have unexplained denominators, missing units, or mislabeled rows, so readers will have to re-derive figures rather than trust the prose.

**Strengths:**

- Navigable structure. The results sections are labeled RQ1–RQ4 (pp.5–11) and map onto the four research questions stated on p.2, and the appendix (methods note plus Tables A1–A6) is bound into the PDF (pp.16–19), so every cross-reference resolves within the document.
- Core descriptive numbers match the tables (checkable). The text on p.5 matches Table 3 (p.6) cell for cell: Black 36%, White 31%, Latino 30%, Asian 23%; grades 9–12 38%, 6–8 30%, K–5 27%; homelessness 50%, disabilities 34%; 67% of school moves accompanied by a residence change, 70% for K–5, 75% for students experiencing homelessness. Table 4's frequency rows sum correctly (21% + 7% + 3% = 31%; "ten percent moved more than once" = 7% + 3%, p.6).
- Figure 1 (p.8) is presented honestly. The y-axis starts at zero, the pandemic period is shaded, and the series decompose cleanly (for 2017–18, roughly 22% once + 9% twice + 5% three or more ≈ 36% any move). The text's "14% ... more than once in 2017–18 compared to 10% in 2023–24" (p.8) can be read off the figure.
- The qualitative component is bounded appropriately. The paper says plainly that interview material from one question was used only to guide specification and interpretation, and that "we do not present the qualitative results as standalone findings" (p.4). This keeps readers from taking the interview-based explanations on pp.6 and 11 as evidence.
- Table 8's note correctly tells readers that Columns A–B are probit marginal effects and Column C holds linear coefficients (p.10), which prevents a common misreading of the count model.
- The distance section states its own measurement limitations directly after the method (zip-code granularity, unknown sequencing of school and residence changes, inability to identify beneficial moves; pp.4–5).

**Weaknesses:**

- **A policy recommendation contradicts the sign of the estimate.** The housing affordability index is defined as "the percentage of households that can afford to purchase a median-priced, single-family home" (p.11), so a higher value means more affordable housing. The coefficient is positive in every reported model: .0013** (p.10, Table 8, Col. A), .0009*/.0037**/.0024** (p.12, Table 9), and positive interactions (p.19, Table A6). The text itself reads this correctly as a 1-point rise in HAI going with "a .13 pp increase in school mobility" (p.11). The discussion nonetheless concludes that "future efforts to reduce school mobility should also focus on ... improving housing affordability" (p.13). By the paper's own estimates, more affordable counties have more mobility, not less.
- **"Consistent across specifications" holds for student variables only (checkable, p.9 vs p.17, Table A3).** Several community-level estimates flip sign across the columns of Table A3. HAI is .0013** with county fixed effects and −.0021** when Los Angeles is excluded. Total foster care facilities is .0095** (w/ Comm) versus −.0387** (w/ Co FE). % multilingual learners is −.0319** (w/ Sch) versus .0305** (w/ Comm). These are the variables the discussion builds policy claims on.
- **The robustness summary for the subgroup tables overstates (checkable, p.11 vs pp.18–19).** The text says changing residence, disability, homelessness, and alternative-school enrollment "remain significant in all three time periods, and this is true across most racial/ethnic groups (Appendix Table A4) and age/grade groups (Appendix Table A5)." The claim holds for residence change and, with one exception (Asian students), for homelessness. For disability, only Black students are significant in all three periods in Table A4, and the middle/high school post-COVID estimate is .0039 (n.s.) in Table A5. For alternative-school enrollment, only Latino students are significant in all three periods in Table A4. In Table A5 neither grade band is: TK–5 pre-COVID is −.0082 and middle/high COVID and post-COVID are .0103 and .0065, all n.s.
- **Causal language outruns a design the authors call correlational.** The abstract calls residential moves "a major driver"; Table 8 is titled "Effects of Student, School, and Community Characteristics" (p.10); the text says changing residence "increases the probability" (p.11) and that facility measures are associated with lower mobility "because they may indicate more placement options" (p.11). Yet p.5 concedes "we cannot determine whether a school change happened before or after they moved."
- **"On average" is used to describe medians.** Table 5 (p.6) reports median distances, but the text says "On average, students relocated 22.5 miles" (pp.6–7) and "On average, students relocate over 20 miles" (p.12). The intro also says "On average ... more than 20 miles" (p.2).
- **Denominators are unexplained or cannot be reconciled (checkable).** Table 5 (residential moves), Table 6 (school moves), and Table A2 all report the same Ns: 49,913 / 20,316 / 9,041 (pp.6, 7, 16). Those Ns do not match Table 4's school-move frequencies. The ratio 20,316/49,913 is about 41%, but Table 4 implies (7% + 3%)/31% ≈ 32% of movers moved more than once. Similarly 9,041/49,913 is about 18% against 3%/31% ≈ 10%.
- **Table 4's destination rows exceed the total.** The rows sum to 9% + 16% + 12% = 37% against 31% who moved, and the table never says whether "different district" includes cross-county moves or how students with multiple moves are counted (p.6).
- **Coefficients lack units, and Table 8 lacks reference categories.** "The child poverty rate is associated with a 5.00 pp increase" (p.11) gives no increment. "Total number of foster care facilities" (−.0387, p.10) has no unit. District enrollment prints as ".0000**" with no scale (Table A3 labels it "in 1,000," p.17). The urbanicity reference group (suburban) appears only in the text (p.11), and the race reference group is never stated.
- **Two production-level table errors that readers can see.** Table 2's "State" row reports 2,929 students in foster care (p.4), which cannot be the state total when p.3 gives 39,099 for 2023–24; it appears to be a county average. Table 9's note prints "p < .05. **p < .01." with the single asterisk missing, and unlike Tables 8, A4, and A5 it does not say whether county and year fixed effects are included (p.12).
- **Contradictory prose on distance trends.** p.7 says "the median distance has risen over time, particularly for third moves," while p.8 says "median travel distance has decreased in recent years, particularly for the first and second residence moves." Both are partly true depending on the baseline year, and a reader must open Figure 3 to reconcile them.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Must-read exhibits:** Table 3 (p.6), Figure 1 (p.8), and Table 8 Column A (p.10) carry most of the paper's argument. Read Table A3 (p.17) alongside Table 8 before citing any school- or community-level coefficient, and look at the "w/o LA" column in particular.
- **Before quoting the post-pandemic community findings**, go to Table 9 (p.12) and Table A6 (p.19) directly. Child poverty's post-COVID estimate (.2070**, Table 9; interaction .1745**, Table A6) supports the abstract's claim. For HAI, the largest estimate is in the COVID period (.0037 vs .0024 post-COVID, Table 9), not after the pandemic, and its positive sign means affordability goes with more mobility.
- **Do not repeat the p.11 robustness sentence about "most racial/ethnic groups" and "age/grade groups"** without checking Tables A4–A5 cell by cell. It holds for residence change and, with one exception, for homelessness. It does not hold for disability or alternative-school enrollment.
- **When citing distances**, say "median distance between residential zip codes among students whose zip code changed" (Table 5, p.6). It is not an average, and it is not the distance from the new home to the school of origin.
- **Treat Tables 5, 6, and A2 as percentage distributions with unclear bases.** Do not use their Ns to compute counts of movers.
- **Figures with no supporting exhibit:** the comparison rates for other student groups (6%, 7%, 8%, 16%; p.5), the between-year figures (35% and 23%; p.4), and the graduation rates (38% vs 60%; p.11) appear only in the prose. Cite them as the authors' statements, not as reported results.
- **Can be skimmed:** the policy background (p.2) and the list of school types (note 7). The "limitations" passage (p.13) is mostly a future-research agenda. The real limitations are on pp.4–5 and in the appendix text (p.16).

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Organization and navigability.* The paper follows a conventional structure and is easy to navigate. The four research questions (p.2) reappear as section labels, the method section defines foster care status (LCFF definition, "at any point during a school year," p.3) and the mobility measure (within-year changes in primary enrollment, p.4) before any results, and the appendix is bound into the document. The load-bearing material is in three places: Table 3 and Figure 1 for the descriptive story, and Table 8 plus Tables A3–A6 for the regressions. The main weakness in navigation is that the regression's sample restrictions are never discussed in the text. Table A3 (p.17) shows the estimation sample shrinking from 304,466 observations (base) to 279,154 (with zip), 251,073 (with school), and 203,095 in the preferred model. Roughly a third of student-years drop out between the descriptive and regression analyses, and the text does not mention it. The unit of analysis also changes silently. Table 1's foster-care N (133,127, p.3) counts unique students, but the all-student N (43,223,355) is about 6.2 million per year over seven years and so must count student-years. Table 3 Column A is per student, Column B is per school move, and Table A3 counts student-years.

*Abstract fidelity.* The abstract's numbers are accurate: 31% overall is implied, the decline "from 36% in 2017–18 to 30% in 2023–24" matches Figure 1 (roughly 35.7% to 30.3%, p.8), and "more than 20 miles" matches Table 5's first-move median of 22.5 (p.6). Four problems remain. First, "residential moves ... serving as a major driver" presents a contemporaneous correlation, whose sequencing the authors say they cannot establish (p.5), as causal. Second, "more likely to transfer to alternative education settings, especially after subsequent moves" has no non-foster comparison for transfers; Table 1 compares enrollment, not transfers. Within Table 6, the traditional-to-alternative share barely moves (14%, 14%, 16%; p.7). The rise across moves is in alternative-to-alternative moves (7% to 18%), which reflects who is already in alternative settings. Third, the abstract does not tell readers that the evidence is descriptive plus a probit with county fixed effects, that the distance measure is zip-to-zip, or that interviews shaped the specification. Fourth, the phrase "some community factors, such as child poverty, became more relevant after the pandemic" is supported for child poverty (Table 9 post-COVID .2070**; Table A6 interaction .1745**). The intro's parallel claim that housing affordability "played a more important role in the post-pandemic period" (p.3) fits less well, since HAI's estimate peaks during the COVID years (p.12, Table 9).

*Fidelity of argument, descriptive sections.* Most of the RQ1 text matches Table 3. One exception is the sentence "Most differences stemmed from disability and homelessness status" (p.5). The disability rate (34%) is only 3 points above the overall 31%, which is a smaller gap than race (Black 36% vs Asian 23%) or grade (38% vs 27%). Only homelessness (50%) is a large departure. The 3-year claim, "over half of students in foster care experienced a midyear school change (Table 3, Column C)," is true of the pooled 52%. But Table A1 (p.16) shows the 3-year rate falling from 58% (2017–18) to 44% (2023–24), so "over half" does not describe recent cohorts. The 3-year window is also never defined. Table A1 reports a 3-year rate for every year from 2017–18 through 2023–24 although the data cover only those seven years (p.3), so the windows at the two ends must be truncated or defined in some way the reader cannot see. The attribution "Because of the frequent placement changes" (p.5) is asserted for a sample in which placements are not observed.

Two RQ2 claims are rounded or undefined. "Approximately 20% of students transitioned from one alternative education setting to another in their third or later move" (p.7) refers to 18% in Table 6. The better-resourced-school finding ("About 30% ... moved from a high-poverty school to a more affluent school," p.7; Table 7, p.8) defines "high-poverty" (at least 75% FRPL) and "high-need" (at least 55% unduplicated) but never defines "affluent" or "low-need." Table 7's denominator is all school-changers, not those starting in high-poverty schools, and the reverse flow (affluent to high-poverty) is not shown, so readers cannot tell whether the movement is net upward. The claims that "most students in foster care attended high-poverty schools" (p.7) and that "most students move between high-poverty schools" (p.13) have no supporting exhibit.

*Fidelity of argument, trends.* The text on Figure 2 (p.8) reports the Black–White gap narrowing from 7 to 5 points and says "the Latino–White gap reversed during the pandemic." The figure (p.9) also shows the Black–White gap reversing in 2020–21, to about −1 point, which the prose omits. The statement that the Latino–White gap is "trending downward in recent years" is ambiguous, because the gap is negative in 2022–23 (about −2) and 2023–24 (about −1.4), so it is moving toward zero. Figure 2's axis is labeled in percent when the quantity is a percentage-point difference. The statement that "all demographic groups have experienced a decrease in school mobility" (p.3) has no single-year exhibit by group behind it, since Figure 2 shows only gaps and Table A1 shows 3-year rates. On distance, Figure 3 (p.9) shows first-move medians rising from roughly 21 to 24 miles by 2020–21 and then easing to about 23. Second-move medians peak near 30 in 2020–21 and return to about 26.5, and third-move medians climb to 35. The p.7 sentence ("risen over time") and the p.8 sentence ("decreased in recent years") describe different windows without saying so. The p.8 text also refers to students "who move three times or more," but the figure's series is the "3rd residential move." Finally, classifying all of 2019–20 as a pandemic year (p.5), and shading it in Figure 1, treats a school year that was mostly in person before March 2020 as "during COVID." The text justifies only the end date of the period, not the start.

*Fidelity of argument, regressions.* Point estimates are transcribed correctly: 44.99 pp, 3.30 pp, 2.13 pp, −1.08 pp, 5.00 pp, and .13 pp (p.11) all match Table 8 Column A (p.10). The interpretation around them is the paper's weakest writing. Beyond the HAI sign problem and the A3–A6 overstatements already listed, three points stand out.

1. The inference that residence change has a smaller effect on multiple moves ("18.57 vs 44.99 pp") and so "additional factors may be at play" (p.11) compares percentage-point effects on outcomes with very different base rates, roughly 10% versus 31% (Table 4). Relative to the base rate, the residence effect is larger for multiple moves.
2. RQ4 promises "student, family, and community factors" (p.2), but Equation (1) (p.5) contains individual, school, and community blocks. No family-level variable is identified as such.
3. Table A6's note says "additional controls include those in Table 8," and Table 8's note says school-year fixed effects are included. Year fixed effects would be perfectly collinear with the COVID and post-COVID period indicators that Table A6 reports (−.1384** and −.0584**, p.19). Either the year effects were dropped or the note is wrong, and the reader cannot tell which. Readers should also note that Table 8's Asian estimate is identical to four decimals in Column A (probit ME, −.0538) and Column C (linear coefficient, −.0538) with different standard errors (.0069 vs .0097). This may be a coincidence, but it is worth checking before relying on the count-model race estimates.

*Tables and figures as self-contained objects.* The figures are the cleanest exhibits. Tables 8 and 9 need the text to be read correctly: they lack units for continuous regressors and reference categories, and Table 8 labels its alternative-school regressor "Primary school is an alternative education setting," which can be misread as elementary school when it means primary enrollment (Table 9 says "School is an alternative education setting"). Grade labels also shift from "K–5" (Tables 3, 5, 7, A1) to "TK-5" (Table A5). Table 2's "State" row reports 2,929 students in foster care and 10 per 1,000. Neither can be a state figure: the state count on p.3 is 39,099 for 2023–24, and 39,099 against about 6.2 million students a year (Table 1's N divided by seven) is roughly 6 per 1,000.

*Density and minor lapses.* At 13 pages of text, the paper is not dense. The discussion (pp.11–13) repeats earlier results and adds new numbers not found in any exhibit, such as the 38% vs 60% graduation comparison. Small production lapses remain: the acronym "EHR" in the text (p.2) versus "ERH" in note 1 (p.13); Brueckner et al. cited as 2021 (p.13) but listed as 2023 (p.14); "Royal Melbourne Institute for Technology" (p.1); the running header "AERA Open 00(0)" on even pages; and typos in the U.S. Department of Education reference title (p.15). None of these affects interpretation. Together with the table-note errors, they suggest the exhibits were not fully re-checked against the final text.

*Bottom line for readers.* The descriptive half of the paper can be quoted with confidence after a glance at the cited table. The regression half, and especially the community-level findings behind the policy recommendations, should be read from Tables 8, 9, and A3–A6 directly rather than from the prose summaries on pp.9–13.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This paper gives a useful, statewide, seven-year descriptive account of within-year school mobility among roughly 133,000 California students in foster care. It adds a few things the literature did not have in one place: a trend series running through the pandemic, a zip-code-based proxy for how far students move when their residence changes, and a tabulation of moves between traditional and alternative school types. Its value is as a descriptive reference for California policy. It is not a source of explanations.
