The headline mobility rate largely updates what California data showed more than a decade ago, and the "first" claims are stated more broadly than they hold up. The regression and pandemic-period findings in the abstract (community poverty and housing affordability "becoming more relevant") are the least robust results in the paper, and one of them is interpreted in a direction its own coefficient does not support.

**Strengths:**

- **Scale and data linkage.** The study links CALPADS enrollment records to the CDSS child-welfare case system (match rate about 94%, p.3) for all seven years from 2017–18 to 2023–24. The sample is 133,127 students in foster care (p.3; Table 1, p.3). Few studies of this population have statewide, multi-year coverage with school identifiers, and this one lets the field track mobility across the pandemic disruption.
- **A clearly defined, policy-relevant outcome.** The paper focuses on within-year (midyear) moves. It justifies that choice (p.4), documents its exclusion rules (p.4; appendix, p.16), and places foster youth against useful comparison groups: 31% versus 6% overall, 7% low-income, and 16% homeless (p.5). As a benchmark, it is well constructed.
- **New descriptive dimensions.** Three of the exhibits are genuinely new relative to the California literature I could check. The first is median zip-to-zip distance per residential move: 22.5, 27.1 and 29.8 miles for first, second and third moves (Table 5, p.6), with trends (Figure 3, p.9). The second is the shift toward alternative settings in later moves: alternative-to-alternative moves rise from 7% of first moves to 18% of third-plus moves (Table 6, Panel A, p.7). The third is where movers go, meaning cross-district or cross-county moves versus moves within a district (Table 4, p.6; Table A2, p.16). These speak directly to the logistics behind ESSA "school of origin" transportation duties.
- **Honest trend reporting.** Figure 1 (p.8) shows the pre-pandemic level (about 36% in 2017–18 and 2018–19), the 2020–21 trough (about 23%), and a partial rebound to about 30–32%. The paper attributes most of the decline to fewer students making multiple moves: 14% moved more than once in 2017–18 versus 10% in 2023–24 (p.8). This is a checkable, useful fact.
- **Subgroup detail that practitioners can use.** Table 3 (p.6) and Table A1 (p.16) give midyear and three-year mobility by race, grade band, disability, homelessness and multilingual status. High schoolers (38%), Black students (36%) and students experiencing homelessness (50%) stand out (Table 3, Col. A). The three-year figure, that over half of students in care experience a midyear move within three years (52%, Table 3, Col. C), is a vivid and defensible statistic.
- **Transparent about data limits.** The paper states that foster-care entry and placement dates are unknown (p.3, p.5), that within-zip moves are missed (p.5), and that private-school and out-of-state moves are not captured (p.16).

**Weaknesses:**

- **Novelty is overstated.** The paper calls itself "the first large-scale analysis of school mobility trends" in California (p.2) and "the first large-scale longitudinal analysis" of the topic (p.11). But WestEd's statewide linked CALPADS–CWS/CMS study of 2009–10 (Barrat & Berliner, 2013, *The Invisible Achievement Gap*) already reported that about one-third of California students in foster care changed schools during the year, and that about 10% attended three or more schools. I verified this from secondary summaries of that report, not the report itself. Gao et al.'s pooled 31% midyear rate and 10% multiple-move rate (Table 4, p.6) are strikingly close to those earlier figures. The paper cites the 2025 WestEd follow-up (Barrat et al., 2025) only for outcomes (p.1) and never benchmarks its level estimates against the earlier California work. What is new is the trend over time, the distance measure and the school-type transitions. The basic level is not new.
- **The "first study to examine how far students in foster care move" claim (p.4) needs qualifying.** The UC Berkeley California Child Welfare Indicators Project already publishes a placement-distance-from-home indicator for California. One reported figure: 39.5% of first entrants in 2014 who stayed in care for 12 months lived 11 or more miles from their removal address. I verified this via Kidsdata; it is not a peer-reviewed study. That indicator measures something different, and the paper's school linkage is new, but readers should not treat this paper as the only distance evidence.
- **The distance statistic is conditional and likely biased upward, and the paper words it loosely.** The distances are medians computed only over moves that change zip code (pp.4–5). Moves within a zip code are dropped by construction, which removes the shortest moves. The paper acknowledges that this undercounts moves (p.5) but not that it inflates the typical distance. The text also says "On average, students relocated 22.5 miles" (pp.6–7), but Table 5 reports medians (checkable). The abstract's "Students typically relocate more than 20 miles" (p.1) therefore describes zip-changing residential moves, not students in care, and not only moves that caused a school change.
- **Regression findings are associations, but they are labeled as effects.** Table 8 is titled "Effects of Student, School, and Community Characteristics on School Mobility" (p.10). The dominant predictor is a same-year residential change, a 44.99 pp marginal effect (Table 8, Col. A, p.10; text p.11), and that variable is jointly determined with the outcome. Given that 67% of school moves coincide with a residence change (Table 3, Col. B, p.6), this coefficient restates the descriptive fact. It is not evidence about a mechanism.
- **The community-level results are fragile, even though the abstract features them.** The text says that "most of the estimates are consistent across specifications" (p.9), but Table A3 (p.17) shows several community coefficients changing sign or size across specifications (checkable):
  - Housing affordability: +.0021 without county FE, +.0013 with county FE, and −.0021 when Los Angeles is excluded.
  - Number of foster care facilities: +.0095 without county FE, −.0387 with county FE.
  - District child poverty: .0158 (n.s.), then .0500, then .0868.

  County-level covariates (the housing affordability index, facility counts, percent STRTPs) are also identified only from within-county year-to-year changes once county fixed effects are included. That is a narrow source of variation, and it does not match the cross-sectional "more placement options" story told on p.11.
- **The housing-affordability interpretation is internally inconsistent.** The housing affordability index (HAI) is defined as the share of households that can afford a median-priced home, so a higher value means more affordable housing (p.11). Its coefficient is positive: a 1 pp increase in the HAI goes with a .13 pp increase in mobility (Table 8, Col. A, p.10; p.11). Yet the Discussion recommends "improving housing affordability" to reduce school mobility (p.13). Taken at face value, the paper's own estimate points the other way (checkable).
- **The post-pandemic poverty finding is thin, and its explanation does not match the evidence.** The district child-poverty coefficient is −.0505 (n.s.) before COVID and .2070** after (Table 9, p.12). The interaction with the post-period is .1745** (Table A6, p.19). The paper explains this with the national near-tripling of child poverty after the expanded Child Tax Credit expired (p.13). But a statewide time shock is absorbed by the year fixed effects. What changed is the cross-district slope within counties, which the national trend does not explain. The effect sizes are also given without units: "a 5.00 pp increase" (p.11) presumably means per full unit of a 0–1 poverty share, which is not stated.
- **The trend is explained with policy stories the data do not test.** The Discussion links the decline to the Family First Prevention Services Act (2018) and California's Continuum of Care Reform (2015) (p.11). But Figure 1 (p.8) shows no pre-pandemic decline (about 36% in both 2017–18 and 2018–19). The drop coincides with the pandemic, and the foster-care population fell 22% over the period (note 3, p.13), so a change in who is in care is a live alternative explanation that the paper does not examine.
- **Key exhibits are ambiguous.** Table 5, which covers residential moves, and Tables 6 and A2, which cover school moves, report identical sample sizes: 49,913 / 20,316 / 9,041 (pp.6–7, p.16; checkable). The implied share of first movers who move again (20,316 / 49,913 ≈ 41%) does not match Table 4's 10% of 31% ≈ 32%. The unit (students or student-years) shifts across tables: Table 1's "All Students" N of 43,223,355 (p.3) can only be student-years. Table 7's "affluent" and "low-need" destinations (p.8) are defined only by the high-poverty and high-need thresholds (p.7), and no reverse-direction flow is reported. As a result, "In some cases, students move to better-resourced schools" (p.1) cannot be read as a net movement toward better schools.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite it for** California's pooled within-year school-mobility rate for students in foster care over 2017–18 to 2023–24: 31%, about five times the 6% general rate (p.5; Table 3, p.6). Also cite it for the subgroup gradients by grade, race, disability and homelessness (Table 3; Table A1). Add the caveat that "in foster care" means in care on any day of the year (p.3), so some counted moves happen before entry or after exit.
- **Cite it for** the descriptive time series: roughly 36% before the pandemic, a 2020–21 trough, and about 30% in 2023–24, with the decline concentrated among students who moved multiple times (Figure 1, p.8; p.8 text).
- **Cite it for** the finding that later midyear moves are more likely to involve alternative settings (Table 6, p.7), and that cross-district and cross-county moves outnumber within-district moves (Table 4, p.6).
- **Cite the distance figures carefully.** Describe them as the median distance between successive residential zip codes among students whose zip code changed, 22.5 miles for the first such move (Table 5, p.6). Do not describe them as the average distance, as how far students in foster care move in general, or as the commute that staying in the school of origin would require.
- **Do not cite it for** the claim that residential or placement changes *cause* school moves, or for magnitudes such as "45 pp." That coefficient mechanically restates a simultaneous correlation (Table 8, p.10).
- **Do not cite it for** "child poverty and housing affordability became more important after the pandemic" as a settled finding. These coefficients are unstable across specifications (Table A3, p.17), and the affordability sign contradicts the policy recommendation (p.11 vs. p.13).
- **Do not cite it for** the claim that the Family First Act, the Continuum of Care Reform, or school-of-origin outreach reduced school mobility (p.11). The design cannot attribute the trend, and the timing in Figure 1 does not support it.
- **Do not cite it for** interview-based mechanisms, such as rural transportation shortages or schools with many students with disabilities providing transportation (p.11), as findings. The paper itself says the qualitative component (seven counties, one interview question) is not a standalone finding (p.4).
- **Open questions it leaves:** how many students stay in their school of origin (acknowledged, p.13); whether moves are best-interest moves or disruptive ones; the effects of mobility on learning; whether the post-pandemic plateau reflects policy or a changed foster-care population; and how well California's patterns carry over to states with state-administered child welfare, different foster-care definitions, or no STRTP transition.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What is genuinely new.* This is a descriptive paper with a regression attached, and it should be judged mainly as a descriptive contribution. Three things are new. First, it extends statewide California evidence on foster-youth school mobility through the pandemic with a consistent definition, so the field has a clean before, during and after series (Figure 1, p.8; Table A1, p.16). Second, the zip-code distance measure (Table 5, p.6; Figure 3, p.9) turns an abstract legal duty into a concrete number: ESSA's requirement that districts arrange transportation to the school of origin. Even with its upward bias, a median above 20 miles for zip-changing moves tells administrators that school-of-origin transportation in California often means cross-district, often cross-county logistics. That is consistent with Table 4's finding that 16% of students moved to a different district and 12% to a different county, versus 9% within the same district (p.6). Third, the school-type transition tables (Table 6, p.7) document a gradient that matters for policy: with each additional midyear move, students are more likely to land in continuation, juvenile court, or other alternative settings. Traditional-to-traditional moves fall from 72% to 54% between first and third-plus moves. No single piece is transformative, but together they are a useful reference for California practitioners and state agencies. The authorship, including California Department of Education staff, also suggests the numbers are close to what the state will act on.

*What is repackaged.* The headline level of mobility is not new. California's own linked data from 2009–10 showed roughly one-third of students in care changing schools during the year, with about 10% attending three or more schools. I verified this from secondary summaries of Barrat & Berliner (2013), so these figures are hedged. Gao et al. report 31% and 10% moving more than once (Table 4, p.6). The definitions probably differ, so the comparison is suggestive, not exact. Still, readers should understand that the paper confirms a long-standing level; it does not uncover a new one. Its framing as "the first large-scale analysis" (p.2) and "first large-scale longitudinal analysis" (p.11) does not engage this predecessor on the level question. Likewise, the finding that about two-thirds of school moves coincide with a residence change (Table 3, Col. B, p.6) explicitly echoes Clemens et al. (2017) and Pears et al. (2015) (p.2). It is a confirmation in a new state, not a discovery.

*Where the most quotable claims outrun the best-supported ones.* The abstract highlights five findings. Two are well supported: foster youth change schools at high rates, and mobility fell from 36% to 30%. One is supported only with qualification: students "typically relocate more than 20 miles." Two are the weakest in the paper: "some community factors, such as child poverty, became more relevant after the pandemic," and "in some cases, students move to better-resourced schools." The distance claim is a median conditional on a zip-code change, and the text calls it an average (pp.6–7). The community-factor claim rests on coefficients that change size and sometimes sign across the specifications in Table A3 (p.17). For county-level covariates, the coefficients are identified only from within-county changes over time once county fixed effects enter. The housing-affordability result is especially risky to cite: the estimated association is positive (more affordable counties show more mobility; Table 8, Col. A, p.10), yet the Discussion recommends improving affordability to reduce mobility (p.13). Readers citing "housing affordability matters for foster youth school mobility" should know the paper's evidence does not tell them in which direction. The "better-resourced schools" claim (Table 7, p.8) is framed without its complement: we are not told what share moved from low-poverty to high-poverty schools. Since most foster youth start in high-poverty schools (p.7), the reported 30% partly reflects where they start.

*The regression's contribution.* Equation (1) (p.5) is a pooled probit of midyear moves on individual, school and community characteristics, with year and county fixed effects. As a descriptive, adjusted profile of who moves, it is informative. Black students (+2.16 pp), students experiencing homelessness (+7.61 pp), students with disabilities (+1.41 pp), and older students remain more mobile after conditioning (Table 8, Col. A, p.10). The Black–White gap narrowed from about 7 to about 5 percentage points (Figure 2, p.9; p.8). These are useful equity facts. But the model has no design for separating causes. Including a same-year residential change as a regressor soaks up much of the variation, and it is not a pre-determined characteristic: in foster care, a placement change often triggers both the residential and the school move at the same time. The analytic sample also shrinks from 304,466 to 203,095 observations (about 67% retained) as school and community covariates are added (Table A3, p.17; checkable), and the paper does not say who drops out. Readers should treat Table 8 as an adjusted description, not as evidence for the levers the Discussion recommends.

*Significance for policy.* The question matters. Federal law (Fostering Connections, 2008; ESSA, 2015) and California law (Continuum of Care Reform, 2015) all aim at educational stability, and the paper's evidence suggests these goals are hard to meet: placements are far away, cross-district moves are common, and repeated movers drift into alternative settings. But the policy-relevant question the laws pose, whether students remain in their school of origin when that is in their best interest, cannot be answered with these data. The paper says so candidly (p.13), and it also cannot separate beneficial moves from harmful ones (p.5). The Discussion's attribution of the trend to prevention and stability policies (p.11) goes past what the data can show. The level was flat before the pandemic (Figure 1, p.8), the drop coincides with distance learning, and the foster-care population fell 22% over the window (note 3, p.13). The policy contribution is therefore mainly diagnostic: it describes the scale and geography of the problem, not what works to address it.

*Generalizability.* The findings are California-specific in several ways the paper does not fully spell out. It uses California's LCFF definition of foster care, which includes probation-supervised and family-maintenance cases (p.3). Child welfare is administered by 58 counties (p.4). The STRTP transition under the Continuum of Care Reform shapes out-of-county placement (p.6). Foster status is coded as in care on any day of the year (p.3), so the "foster youth" rate mixes moves before entry, during care, and after exit. The pooled 31% should therefore be read as "school mobility among students touched by foster care in a given year" rather than "mobility while in care." Comparisons with states that measure mobility during placement spells (e.g., Clemens et al., 2017) should allow for that difference. The exclusion of private-school and out-of-state moves (p.16) probably biases mobility downward slightly, and the zip-code method biases distances upward.

*Standing in the literature and follow-on work.* This is now probably the most current and comprehensive published descriptive source on midyear school mobility for California foster youth, and a reasonable citation for the post-pandemic level and trend. It is not the best evidence on the consequences of mobility (Pears et al., 2015; Clemens et al., 2018 remain the references there). Nor is it the best evidence on the link between placement changes and school changes, where Clemens et al. (2017) has actual placement records while this paper uses zip-code proxies. The most valuable follow-on work it sets up is concrete. Linking placement-spell dates and school-of-origin fields would let researchers measure stability *while in care*. The distance and school-type patterns could be used to study whether cross-district transportation agreements (mentioned for large counties, p.13) actually keep students in place. And an event-study design around placement changes could replace the simultaneous residential-change regressor. Replication will depend on CDE data access (Open Practices, p.13), which limits independent verification of the tables flagged above.

*Bottom line.* This is a modest but useful contribution on an important question: a solid descriptive update with some genuinely new exhibits. Its framing and several highlighted secondary findings claim more than the evidence supports. The Adequate rating reflects a real descriptive contribution alongside novelty claims and community-factor conclusions that readers should discount.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (low confidence)

The study rests on restricted CALPADS records linked to child-welfare data, and the Open Practices statement names a real CDE application pathway. The regression exhibits are unusually complete: every column reports standard errors and sample sizes, there is a six-column specification ladder, and all the regression numbers quoted in the text match the tables. But the code is available only on request, only to researchers CDE has already approved, and no software environment is reported. Several construction steps a replicator would need are left undocumented: the unit of analysis in the descriptive tables, why roughly a third of student-years drop out of the regression sample, the scaling of covariates, the type of marginal effect, and how the public covariates were built and aligned in time. A reader with CDE access could approximately rebuild the headline mobility rates and the preferred probit. Exact replication of several descriptive exhibits and some of the community-level coefficients would take guesswork. The rating sits near the boundary with Weak.

**Strengths:**

- **The data access pathway is real and named.** The Open Practices statement (p.13) points to https://www.cde.ca.gov/ds/da/researchdata.asp. As of the review date, that page describes a formal process: a concept paper, a check against CDE research priorities, an intake form, and a data-sharing MOU. It also lists hourly processing fees. Because the student data are FERPA-protected, not posting them is legitimate and is not held against the paper.
- **Core constructs are defined in plain terms.** Foster status follows the LCFF definition and counts a student as in care at any point in the year (p.3). School mobility means more than one primary-enrollment school within a year, with named exclusions: dropouts, suspensions, short enrollments, summer moves, and concurrent enrollment (p.4; appendix p.16, including the 5-day rule affecting "about 175 students"). The linkage is described too: a CDE–CDSS statewide match at about 94%, with tribal-court youth identified separately (p.3).
- **Equation (1) is fully written out.** It is a probit on individual, start-of-year school, and start-of-year community covariates with school-year fixed effects (p.5). The paper states that county fixed effects enter the preferred model and that standard errors are clustered at the student level (p.5; Table 8 note, p.10). It also states the start-of-year convention for students who move (p.5, p.9; Table A3 note, p.17).
- **The specification ladder is transparent.** Table A3 (p.17) adds covariate blocks one at a time: base, residential change, school, community, county FE, and excluding LA. Each column has its own N. **Checkable:** Table A3 Col. 5 ("w/ Co FE") reproduces Table 8 Col. A (p.10) for the rows I compared, including Asian −.0538, Black .0216, residential change .4499, child poverty .0500, HAI .0013, and N = 203,095.
- **The text matches the tables.** **Checkable:** the in-text effect sizes on p.11 match Table 8 (p.10): residential change 44.99 pp (Col. A .4499), alternative setting 3.30 pp (.0330), rural 2.13 pp (.0213), urban −1.08 pp (−.0108), child poverty 5.00 pp (.0500), HAI .13 pp (.0013), and multiple moves 18.57 pp (Col. B .1857). The Table 4 move counts sum to the headline rate: 21% + 7% + 3% = 31% (p.6).
- **The subgroup Ns fit together.** **Checkable:** the three period-specific Ns in Table 9 (p.12; 62,609 + 57,105 + 83,341) sum to 203,055. The six grade-band Ns in Table A5 (p.19) sum to exactly the same 203,055. This is 40 fewer than the pooled 203,095, which is consistent with a few observations dropped for perfect prediction.
- **The figure-based claims match the figures.** Checked against the rendered pages:
  - Figure 1 (p.8) shows about 36% mobility in 2017–18 and 2018–19 and about 30% in 2023–24.
  - Moving twice or more is roughly 9% + 5% ≈ 14% in 2017–18 and roughly 7% + 3% ≈ 10% in 2023–24, as the text on p.8 says.
  - Figure 2 (p.9) shows a Black–White gap of about 7 pp falling to about 5 pp.
  - Figure 3 (p.9) shows a third-move median of about 35 miles in 2023–24.
- **All covariate sources are named in the table source notes.** They are listed in full under Tables 8 and 9 (pp.10, 12): NCES School Geocodes, Census SAIPE, California DOJ crime data, the C.A.R. Housing Affordability Index, and CDSS facility data. All are real, publicly reachable sources.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The code is effectively not shared.** Do-files go only to "approved users" via "methods approved by the California Department of Education" (p.13). FERPA protects student records, not analysis code, so the stated rationale does not obviously cover the code. There is no deposited package, no software or version statement (the word "do-files" implies Stata, but the paper never says so), no codebook, and no synthetic or example data. By journal-era norms this is below expectations.
- **About a third of the analytic sample disappears without explanation.** **Checkable:** Table A3 (p.17) N falls from 304,466 (Base) to 279,154 (adding residential change), 251,073 (adding school covariates), and 203,125 (adding community covariates). The paper never says which variables are missing or for whom. Separately, the appendix drops students with "inconsistent birthdays and incomplete enrollment records" (p.16) but does not report how many.
- **The Ns across Table 8 columns are unexplained.** **Checkable:** Col. A has 203,095 observations, Col. B 207,042, and Col. C 207,046 (p.10). Col. C is a linear model with the same covariates plus county FE, yet it has about 3,900 more observations than the probit without county FE in Table A3 Col. 4 (203,125). No note explains this.
- **The unit of analysis in the descriptive tables is never stated.** Readers cannot tell whether a table counts students, student-years, or moves.
  - **Checkable:** Table 1 (p.3) reports 133,127 foster students against 43,223,355 "All Students." The second figure is about 6.2 million per year over seven years, so it appears to count student-years, while the first counts unique students.
  - Tables 5, 6, and A2 (pp.6, 7, 16) report identical Ns (49,913 / 20,316 / 9,041), even though Table 5 describes *residential* moves and Tables 6 and A2 describe *school* moves.
  - Those Ns imply that 41% of first movers had a second move (20,316/49,913). Table 4 implies about 32% (10/31 of movers).
  - The destination shares in Table 4 (9% + 16% + 12% = 37%, against 31% who moved) cannot be reconciled with the per-move shares in Table A2 (40% different district, 28% different county) from what is reported.
- **The three-year mobility measure is undefined.** Table 3 Col. C (p.6) and Table A1 (p.16) report "3-year period" rates for every year from 2017–18 through 2023–24. A backward window for 2017–18 would need data from before the stated coverage (p.3), and a forward window for 2023–24 would need data after it. The paper does not say which window it uses or whether windows are truncated.
- **Covariate construction and scaling are underspecified.**
  - Units are missing for child poverty (a proportion or a percent?), facility counts, and district enrollment. Table 8 prints district enrollment as ".0000**", and in Table A3 the same variable appears as "(in 1,000)".
  - The equation text refers to "crime rates in the city" (p.5), but the tables use "Number of crimes (in 1,000)" (pp.10, 12, 17).
  - The paper does not say how students or schools are mapped to a city (including unincorporated areas), or how calendar-year and quarterly sources (SAIPE, C.A.R. HAI) are aligned to school years.
  - The school geocodes are a single 2023–24 vintage used for all seven years (Table 8 source note).
  - "% Highly mobile students," "affluent school," and "low-need school" are not defined (pp.7–8, Table 7).
  - The reference categories for race and school type are not stated.
- **The estimand is ambiguous.** The paper never says whether the marginal effects are average marginal effects or evaluated at the means, or whether dummies are treated as discrete changes. Table A6 (p.19) reports "marginal effects" of interaction terms in a probit without saying how they were computed. This matters for the post-COVID poverty claim, which rests on the interaction .1745** (p.19).
- **The distance measure is not replayable.** Distances were "computed via Google Maps API" between ZIP codes (p.4). The paper does not specify driving versus straight-line distance, the point used for each ZIP (centroid or otherwise), the query date, or how out-of-state ZIPs were handled. The results depend on the API's state at query time.
- **The qualitative component cannot be verified.** It covers 50+ interviews, one question, and inductive thematic analysis (p.4), and it is credited with guiding the regression specification. No protocol, codebook, breakdown of interviewees by role, or theme summary is provided. Table 2's "State" row lists 2,929 students in foster care (p.4). That matches neither the state total of about 39,099 (p.3) nor a 58-county mean, and it is not explained.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Lean most on what the paper documents best.** That is the pooled descriptive rates in Tables 3–4, the trend in Figure 1, and the Table 8 Col. A residential-change, homelessness, and disability coefficients. These match across text, tables, and figures, and they are stable across the Table A3 ladder.
- **Treat the community-level findings as weakly verifiable.** This covers housing affordability, crime, and facility counts. **Checkable** (Table A3, p.17):
  - HAI changes sign from .0013** (Col. 5) to −.0021** (Col. 6, excluding LA).
  - Crime moves from .0000 to −.0003**.
  - Total foster facilities is .0095** without county FE (Col. 4) and −.0387** with it (Col. 5).
  - The text on p.9 nonetheless calls most estimates "consistent across specifications."
- **Read Table 9 with its fixed effects unconfirmed.** Its note does not state which fixed effects are included, while the notes to Tables A4 and A5 do. A replicator should confirm that Table 9 uses the same county and year FE as Table 8.
- **Ask the authors for a missingness table** covering the drop from 304,466 to 203,095 observations, broken down by school type. If the community covariates are missing mostly for county-operated alternative schools (for example, because SAIPE district poverty estimates do not cover county offices of education), the alternative-setting and community estimates come from a selected sample. This is a hypothesis; the paper does not report enough to confirm or rule it out.
- **Check the HAI coverage yourself.** Recent C.A.R. Housing Affordability Index releases track 53 counties, not all 58. Check which counties had HAI in 2017–24, and whether the rest were dropped or imputed.
- **Plan to re-estimate distances.** A replicator should use a documented, stable method such as Census ZCTA centroids with great-circle distance, and treat the paper's Table 5 medians as approximate.
- **Do not attempt to replicate the Table 5/6/A2 counts or the three-year rates without first getting the denominators and window definitions from the authors.** As printed, they are not reconstructible.
- **Budget for access.** Would-be replicators need the CDE application (concept paper, MOU, fees). They should confirm up front that the foster-care match flag and residential ZIP histories are included in the files they would receive; the CDE page does not say. They then need to request the do-files separately. Three of the five authors are CDE staff, so the path outsiders face is not the one the authors used.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Data availability.* This paper is a typical case of restricted state administrative data. The student-level CALPADS records, and the CWS/CMS-derived foster flags linked to them, cannot be posted, and the paper correctly cites FERPA (p.13). The named access route exists and is formal. The CDE research-data page requires a concept paper aligned with departmental research priorities and an executed data-sharing agreement, and it charges processing fees. So the pathway is real, but it is discretionary and costly, and approval is not guaranteed. The five public covariate sources are all genuine and publicly reachable:

- SAIPE school-district estimates of children aged 5–17 in poverty
- NCES EDGE school geocodes
- California DOJ crime statistics
- C.A.R.'s county Housing Affordability Index
- CDSS Community Care Licensing facility data

The authors could have posted the merged district-, city-, and county-by-year covariate file they built from these public sources without any FERPA concern. They did not, so a replicator must rebuild it from scratch without knowing the merge keys, the time alignment, or the scaling. That merged file matters more for verification than it might seem, because the paper's most policy-relevant new claim runs through those covariates: child poverty and housing affordability "became more relevant after the pandemic" (abstract, p.1; Table A6, p.19).

*Code.* The Open Practices statement offers do-files only to researchers who have already secured CDE approval, and delivers them through CDE-approved channels (p.13). This is more restrictive than "available upon request," and the justification given (FERPA) applies to records, not scripts. Journal-era norms call for a deposited package, or at least posted code with an explicit reason it cannot run without the restricted data. The paper provides neither, and it names no software or version. For a probit with county FE, a student-clustered variance estimator, and marginal effects, the defaults of the estimating command (for example, how margins treat factor variables, or how observations perfectly predicted by fixed effects are dropped) directly shape the reported numbers and the Ns.

*Rebuilding the analytic file.* The mobility definition is the paper's best-documented element. The appendix (p.16) gives the county-district-school identifier, the primary-enrollment rule, the 5-day exclusion, and the treatment of dropouts, suspensions, summer moves, and concurrent enrollment. A replicator would still have to guess at several steps:

- How summer boundaries are set.
- How re-enrollment in the same school after an exit is handled.
- Whether moves into juvenile court schools (incarceration-driven) are counted like any other move. They appear to be, given Table 6 Panel B (p.7).
- How the residential-ZIP history is built. CALPADS records addresses "throughout the year" (p.4), but the timing of updates is not given. If ZIPs are refreshed mainly when a new enrollment record is created, detected residential changes will cluster at school changes by construction. Only the construction code would settle this.

*Denominators.* The descriptive exhibits are where reproducibility is thinnest. The paper moves between students, student-years, and moves without saying which one a table uses.

- Table 1 compares 133,127 foster students with 43.2 million "All Students," a figure that fits student-years.
- Tables 5, 6, and A2 share one set of Ns even though they describe different events (residential versus school moves).
- Those Ns do not match the Table 4 distribution of moves.
- The three-year measure in Table 3 Col. C and Table A1 has no stated window, yet it has values for the first and last years of a seven-year panel.

None of these points necessarily shows an error; each could have a benign explanation. But a replicator cannot tell which, and so cannot know whether a failure to match is their mistake or the paper's.

*Specification and results.* The regression side is considerably better. Equation (1), the covariate list, the FE structure, the clustering, and the start-of-year convention are stated. Table 8 reports three outcome definitions with SEs and Ns. Table A3 shows how the estimates change as each block is added, and the coefficients I checked match between Table A3 Col. 5 and Table 8 Col. A. The subgroup Ns in Tables 9 and A5 sum consistently. Two gaps remain. The first is the estimand: the type of marginal effect, and how the Table A6 "marginal effects" of interactions were computed, which is non-trivial in a probit. The second is scaling: a coefficient of −.0387 on a raw facility count within a county, or .0000** on district enrollment, cannot be interpreted or reproduced without units. The specification ladder also exposes fragility the text understates, most notably the sign reversal of the HAI coefficient when LA is excluded (Table A3, p.17). Readers can check that directly from the published exhibit, and it should temper reliance on the housing-affordability narrative in the Discussion (p.13).

*Qualitative input.* The interviews are presented not as findings but as guides to model specification (p.4). That makes them part of the analytic pipeline, yet nothing about them is reportable or checkable: no protocol, no codebook, no themes, and no count of interviewees by role. Readers should treat the interview-based explanations (for example, rural transport constraints, p.11) as the authors' interpretation rather than as evidence.

*Bottom line.* This is an honest descriptive study with a legitimate reason not to share data, a real access pathway, and regression exhibits that hold together internally. A replicator with CDE access would probably reproduce the headline rates (31% overall, and the decline from about 36% to about 30%) and the large residential-change association. The same replicator would likely fail to match the move-level descriptive Ns, the three-year rates, the distance medians, and possibly the community-covariate coefficients without help from the authors. That profile fits Adequate, held at the low end: the central results can be understood and approximately verified, but a meaningful share of the exhibits are not reconstructible as printed.
